newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan ends controls on foreign currency transfers.
newsitem.headline: Jordan ends controls on foreign currency transfers.

text.p: Jordan's Central Bank on Sunday announced it had lifted all controls on foreign currency transfers to boost foreign investments and enhance confidence in the local currency.
Jordan Central Bank Governor, Ziyad Fariz, said the move taken by the bank's board was a further step towards liberalisation of the financial sector.
He said it did away with all restrictions on amounts of foreign currency which Jordanians and local corporations can transfer or invest abroad.
"There are no longer any foreign exchange controls whatsoever, (there is) free movement of capital," Fariz told Reuters.
Free movement of capital was previously restricted to expatriate Jordanians who held non-resident foreign currency accounts and foreigners bringing in foreign currency.

"Foreign and local investors have now full freedom to get their money in and out in any currency without any restrictions. This assures them that when they bring their money to Jordan they can also take it back," said Mifleh Aqel regional manager at Jordan's leading Arab Bank.
Central Bank officials expect the move to further bolster the dinar which has since 1995 been fixed at 0.709 to the dollar by raising confidence in the financial system and hampering any outflows.
"The dinar has now become fully convertible," said another Central Bank official, adding that it would remain pegged to the same dollar value.
Officials said the measures now lift a ceiling equivalent to 500,000 dinars on foreign currency deposits which a single Jordanian can hold in domestic banks.
It similarly abolishes ceiling equivalent to 1 million dinars on company deposits in foreign currency.
Only foreigners resident in Jordan were allowed to deposit unlimited amounts of foreign currency in a Jordanian bank account without restrictions on transfers.
The move also abolishes a 5,000 dinar ceiling on dinar bank notes which now can be carried outside the country without prior Central Bank approval.
"A Jordanian could now get out a million dinars in bank notes at the airport and no one would say anything," an official said.

The new rules end restrictions on amounts transferred by Jordanians for personal needs by lifting a ceiling of around $50,000 in annual expenses for medical, education, pilgrimage and family assistance.
It also for the first time allows free movement of capital by Jordanians for investment purposes.

Prior to the move Jordanian companies investing capital abroad had to seek approval on a case by case basis and it was technically not legal for ordinary Jordanians to invest in capital markets abroad.
Most of the limits had been imposed after a sharp devaluation of the dinar in 1989, sparked by an economic crisis.

Bankers say the Central Bank was encouraged in the timing of the move after net foreign currency cash reserves reached $1 billion, or close to the 1997 target, after record inflows of capital in the first half of the year.
"The move was taken after the Central Bank was assured of the dinar's exchange rate and that its reformist policy succeeded in building the reserves to comfortable levels," Aqel said.
